946.title: Modern close: saints now
946.hook: holiness keeps showing up in every generation, including this one
946.howItsDone: Catholics celebrate All Saints' Day for the holy dead known and unknown, ask the saints for their prayers, and in parishes and families tell the stories of holy people they have known.

segments.voice: Yesterday, new movements: a hearth in a bomb shelter, students in Rome, a war ended by talks. Your line was laypeople lead. When does the group you looked up meet next? Day nine hundred forty-six.

This stretch of the path began in a French village, with a country priest, the Curé of Ars, hearing confessions from morning until night. Since then: a priest among the lepers of Molokai. Bakhita, sold as a slave and later a Canossian sister. A young Carmelite writing Story of a Soul. A friar in a starvation cell at Auschwitz. A mother named Gianna. An archbishop at the altar in San Salvador. A pope in an empty square. A teenager with a website. Today closes the modern Church with one question, asked plainly: are there saints now?
screen: `FROM A VILLAGE PRIEST IN ARS…` → `…TO A TEENAGER WITH A WEBSITE.` → `ARE THERE SAINTS NOW?`

segments.voice: First, the Church's own answer. The Second Vatican Council gave a whole chapter of its teaching on the Church to what it called the universal call to holiness: every baptized person, not only priests and religious, is called to be holy, in a kitchen, an office, a hospital ward. Saint Paul says it to the Thessalonians, in the Douay-Rheims: "For this is the will of God, your sanctification." Sanctification means being made holy. Not someday, and not only for experts. Second, the saints next door. Pope Francis wrote a letter on holiness in which he spoke of the saints next door: parents raising their children with love, people working hard to support their families, the sick, elderly religious who keep smiling. Holiness, he wrote in effect, is found among our neighbors. Third, canonized and not. When the Church canonizes someone, it declares that this person is with God and can be held up as a model. But the Church does not teach that heaven holds only the canonized. The feast of All Saints honors the whole crowd, named and unnamed. And some people in this stretch of the path, like Dorothy Day, still have causes open; the Church hasn't finished looking. Fourth, they're still here. In Catholic belief the saints are not gone but alive in God, joined with the living in what the creed calls the communion of saints. Catholics ask for their prayers the way they'd ask a friend. So the line for today means two things at once. The saints of the past are alive in God. And, the Church teaches, new ones are walking around now, in this generation, mostly unnoticed, maybe on your street.
screen: `A CALL TO HOLINESS FOR EVERYONE.` · `THE SAINTS NEXT DOOR.` · `CANONIZED, AND NOT.` · `THE COMMUNION OF SAINTS.` · then, large: `THIS IS THE WILL OF GOD, YOUR SANCTIFICATION.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice a holy person you know. Settle, and breathe. Let someone come to mind whose goodness you've seen up close: a grandparent, a nurse, a neighbor, a teacher, a friend who keeps showing up. Not a perfect person. Just someone good in a way that stays with you. Picture one ordinary moment of theirs: their hands at work, a phrase they always say, the way they make room for people. Stay with that moment. If you pray, you can thank God for them by name. If you don't, simply be grateful for them, slowly. The bell holds the time.
Modern close. The end of this stretch on the modern Church, from the Curé of Ars to a teenager with a website: holiness showing up in every generation, including this one.
Your line: they're still here. Today, tell the person you thought of one good thing you've seen in them, plainly, without making a speech. Day nine hundred forty-six.

947.title: The calendar of saints
947.hook: the Church's book of saints lists holy people for every day of the year
947.howItsDone: The Roman Martyrology lists saints and blesseds for each day of the year; in some monasteries and religious houses a portion is read aloud each day, and some Catholics check the day's saints in a calendar or app.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the modern Church with the saints of now, and your line was they're still here. Did a holy person you know come to mind? Today a new stretch of the climb begins: saints across the calendar. Day nine hundred forty-seven.

In some monasteries, at the morning gathering, a reader stands and reads something that sounds like a list of headlines from a very old newspaper. A place, a name, a few words about a life. At Rome, a martyr. In Gaul, a bishop. In Egypt, a hermit. The names keep coming, from different centuries and different corners of the map, and then the reading stops and the day begins. Nobody in the room knew most of these people. Tomorrow there will be a fresh list. That book has a name, and it's today's word.
screen: `A READER AT THE MORNING GATHERING.` → `A PLACE, A NAME, A FEW WORDS.` → `TOMORROW, A FRESH LIST.`

segments.voice: The book is the Roman Martyrology. It is the Church's official calendar of saints, arranged by days of the year, so that every date carries its own names. The word martyr sits right inside it, and earlier on this climb you met that word as witness. So start with the job Jesus gives his friends in the Acts of the Apostles, just before he ascends, in the Douay-Rheims: "you shall be witnesses unto me in Jerusalem, and in all Judea, and Samaria, and even to the uttermost part of the earth." Notice the map in that sentence: a city, then a region, then the ends of the earth. The Martyrology reads like that map filled in. Tradition says the book began with those who died for their witness, and it grew to hold every kind of holy life. Bishops, nurses, farmers, teachers, mothers, kings, children. The entries are short on purpose. A place first, then a name, then a line or two. Some saints get a sentence; many get a phrase. Reading it, you meet people you've never heard of, from towns you can't find, and each one is set down as worth remembering on this exact day. The book also admits what it can't hold. Its daily lists traditionally end by remembering the many other holy people, unnamed, whose lives only God knows. That honest gap matters. The Martyrology is not a hall of fame. It's a reminder that holiness is crowded. No date on the calendar is empty of it. For the next stretch of this climb, we'll walk through the year by that calendar, meeting one saint at a time, and learning how the Church decides who goes in the book.
screen: `THE CHURCH'S BOOK OF SAINTS, DAY BY DAY.` · `TO THE UTTERMOST PART OF THE EARTH.` · `A PLACE, A NAME, A LINE OR TWO.` · `AND MANY OTHERS, UNNAMED.` · then, large: `YOU SHALL BE WITNESSES UNTO ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look up today's saints. If you have a phone nearby, search for today's date and the word saints, or open a Catholic calendar, and find one name you don't know. Read just the line or two about them. Then put the phone down and settle into the sit. Let that one stranger's name rest with you. Where did they live? What did they do with their ordinary days? If you pray, you can ask that saint to pray for you. If you don't, simply hold the name, and the fact that someone remembered it. The bell holds the time.
Martyrology. The Church's calendar of saints, a list of holy people for each day of the year, with names from every corner of the map.
Your line: every day, someone. Today, when you check the date on anything, a receipt, a screen, a form, remember that the calendar has a name written on it somewhere. Day nine hundred forty-seven.

948.title: How someone becomes a saint
948.hook: a life examined, then usually miracles investigated, then a declaration
948.howItsDone: A cause for canonization usually opens in the diocese where the person died, gathers testimony and writings, goes to the Vatican's Dicastery for the Causes of Saints, and, usually after an investigated miracle, ends with the pope declaring the person a saint at a canonization Mass.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was martyrology, the Church's calendar of saints, and your line was every day, someone. Whose name did you find for your date? Today: how a name gets into that book. Day nine hundred forty-eight.

Somewhere in an office in Rome, there are boxes of paper about a woman who died in a small town. Letters she wrote. Interviews with neighbors who knew her. A doctor's report about a sick child who recovered after people asked her to pray for the child. Someone has read every page. Someone else has argued against her, on purpose, looking for the weak spots. It might take years. It might take longer than anyone in the town lives. All of it is to answer one question carefully. That slow, careful answer is today's word.
screen: `BOXES OF PAPER ABOUT ONE LIFE.` → `SOMEONE ARGUES AGAINST HER, ON PURPOSE.` → `ONE QUESTION, ANSWERED SLOWLY.`

segments.voice: Canonization is the Church's formal declaration that a person is a saint: that they are with God, and that they can be honored and asked for prayers by the whole Church. The first thing to know is what it doesn't do. In Catholic teaching, canonization doesn't make anyone holy. It recognizes a holiness that was already there. The Church says it is declaring, not creating. The second thing is how slow it is. A cause usually begins in the diocese where the person died, when the bishop there agrees to open it. Then comes the examination of the life: writings read, witnesses heard, the whole story laid out. The question is whether this person lived the virtues, faith, hope and love, along with prudence, justice, courage and self-control, to a heroic degree. Jesus gave a test for that kind of thing in the Sermon on the Mount, in the Douay-Rheims: "By their fruits you shall know them." The investigators are looking for fruit. Next, usually, comes a miracle: a healing, for instance, that doctors examine and cannot explain, after people asked this person to pray for them. The Church treats that as a sign that the person is with God. For martyrs, the process can differ, but the investigation is still real. And through all of it, objections get a hearing: an official's task is to raise them. Older tradition nicknamed that role the devil's advocate. Only at the end does the pope make the declaration, at a Mass, using a formal statement that this person is a saint. Tested first. Then declared.
screen: `DECLARING, NOT CREATING.` · `A LIFE EXAMINED FOR HEROIC VIRTUE.` · `USUALLY, A MIRACLE INVESTIGATED.` · `THEN THE POPE DECLARES.` · then, large: `BY THEIR FRUITS YOU SHALL KNOW THEM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read a saint's cause online. Before the sit, or after it, search the name of someone whose cause is open, perhaps someone from your own country or city, and read what the people who knew them said. For now, settle in. Bring to mind one person you've known whose life bore good fruit. Don't declare anything about them. Just notice the fruit: a patience, a kindness, a way they treated people nobody noticed. If you pray, you can give thanks for them. If not, let them stay with you for a while. The bell holds the time.
Canonization. The Church's formal declaration, after a long examination, that a person is a saint, to be honored by the whole Church.
Your line: tested, then declared. Today, before you praise or judge something quickly, give it the slow treatment: one more look, one more question. Day nine hundred forty-eight.

949.title: Venerable and blessed
949.hook: steps along the way: Servant of God, Venerable, Blessed, Saint
949.howItsDone: A cause moves through the titles Servant of God, Venerable, Blessed and Saint; beatification Masses are usually held in the Blessed's home region, and the feast of a Blessed is kept locally.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was canonization, and your line was tested, then declared. Did you give anything the slow treatment? Today, the steps before that declaration. Day nine hundred forty-nine.

On a parish noticeboard, a small printed card: a photograph of a nun in an old-fashioned habit, and underneath, her name, with the words Servant of God in front of it. A few streets away, a church window shows a priest with Blessed before his name. Neither is called saint. Both are clearly on their way somewhere. Those titles are not decoration. Each one marks a step on a long road, and the step in the middle has its own word.
screen: `SERVANT OF GOD, ON A NOTICEBOARD.` → `BLESSED, IN A CHURCH WINDOW.` → `STEPS ON A LONG ROAD.`

segments.voice: Yesterday you heard about the whole process. Today, the titles along the way, because each one tells you exactly where a person stands. The first is Servant of God. It begins when a cause is officially opened. It makes no judgment yet; it only says the Church has started looking. The second is Venerable. That comes when the pope approves a decree that this person lived the virtues to a heroic degree. People may now point to that life as an example. The third is Blessed, and the step that gives that title is today's word: beatification. It comes from the Latin beatus, the word the Latin Bible uses for blessed in the Beatitudes. In the Douay-Rheims, they begin: "Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven." For beatification, the Church usually requires a miracle, examined carefully, after people asked the Venerable person to pray for them. Martyrs are the exception; their death for the faith can be enough for this step. Once beatified, a Blessed can be honored publicly, but usually in a particular place: a diocese, a country, a religious community. Their feast is kept there, not everywhere. The final step is canonization, which opens that honor to the whole Church. So a Blessed is honored at home; a Saint is honored everywhere. Some people stay at one of these steps for a long time, sometimes for good, and that's not a verdict on their lives. It's simply where the examination has reached. The long line keeps moving, one careful step at a time.
screen: `SERVANT OF GOD: THE CAUSE IS OPEN.` · `VENERABLE: HEROIC VIRTUE APPROVED.` · `BLESSED: HONORED IN A PARTICULAR PLACE.` · `SAINT: HONORED BY THE WHOLE CHURCH.` · then, large: `BLESSED ARE THE POOR IN SPIRIT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn one Blessed from your country. Later today, search for the word Blessed and the name of your country or region, and pick one life to read about. For now, settle into the sit. Think of the place where you live: its streets, its churches, its hospitals and schools. Somewhere in its history, someone may have lived quietly in a way their neighbors never forgot. If you pray, you can ask God for the holiness of your own place. If not, simply hold your town in mind, gently, for a while. The bell holds the time.
Beatification. The step that declares a person Blessed, usually after a miracle, so they can be honored publicly in a particular place.
Your line: the long line. Today, notice something good that's only partway done, yours or someone else's, and let it be partway without judging it. Day nine hundred forty-nine.

950.title: Relics, honestly
950.hook: Catholics honor the remains of saints as signs of holy lives, not magic
950.howItsDone: Catholic churches often keep relics of saints in altars or reliquaries; on feast days relics may be exposed for veneration, and people may kneel, pray nearby or touch the reliquary, while Church law forbids selling relics.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was beatification, the step that makes someone Blessed, and your line was the long line. What did you find that was only partway done? Day nine hundred fifty.

A grandmother's wedding ring, kept in a drawer. A father's reading glasses, still on the shelf years later. A child's first shoe. Nobody thinks the ring has powers. Nobody prays to the glasses. But nobody throws them away either, because they were close to someone who mattered, and touching them brings that person near. Hold that drawer in mind. It's the honest way into a word that makes some people uneasy, the word for what Catholics keep from the saints.
screen: `A RING IN A DRAWER.` → `GLASSES STILL ON THE SHELF.` → `CLOSE TO SOMEONE WHO MATTERED.`

segments.voice: A relic is something that remains from a saint: a piece of the body, often a fragment of bone, or something the saint used or wore. Catholics keep relics in churches, in altars, in small glass cases called reliquaries, and honor them. Honor is the key word. In Catholic teaching, relics are venerated, not worshipped. Worship belongs to God alone. A relic is honored because of the person it points to, and because of what Catholics believe about the body: that it was a temple of the Holy Spirit and will rise again. The Psalms put the feeling simply, in the Douay-Rheims: "Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints." The Bible also has stories that sit behind the practice. In the books of Kings, a dead man is lowered into the grave of the prophet Elisha, touches his bones, and comes back to life. In the Acts of the Apostles, cloths that had touched Paul are carried to the sick, and they recover. Catholics read those as God acting through holy people, even through what they leave behind. Now the honest part. Relics have been faked, stolen, sold and fought over. The Church's own teaching warns against superstition, against treating any object as if it worked by itself, like a charm. Church law forbids selling relics at all. So a relic, rightly understood, is not a lucky object. It's closer to that drawer at home. A body, or a thing, that once belonged to someone who loved God, kept close so the memory stays warm.
screen: `WHAT REMAINS FROM A SAINT.` · `VENERATED, NOT WORSHIPPED.` · `ELISHA'S BONES, PAUL'S CLOTHS.` · `NOT A CHARM; NEVER FOR SALE.` · then, large: `PRECIOUS IN THE SIGHT OF THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: visit a church's relic. Some churches have one in or under the altar, or in a side chapel; when you can, go and stand in front of it for a minute. For now, in the sit, think of an object you've kept because of someone you loved. See it clearly: its weight, its color, where it lives in your home. Let the person come to mind through it. If you pray, you can pray for them, or ask a saint to pray with you. If not, hold the object and the person together, quietly. The bell holds the time.
Relic. Something that remains from a saint, their body or something they used, honored for the holy life it points to, never worshipped.
Your line: bodies that loved god. Today, treat one ordinary body with honor, your own included: a rest, a meal eaten slowly, a hand held. Day nine hundred fifty.

951.title: Patron saints
951.hook: Catholics ask particular saints to pray for particular needs
951.howItsDone: Catholics ask patron saints to pray for them in particular needs, places or kinds of work; parishes and countries keep their patron's feast, and some people keep a patron's image or medal at work or at home.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was relic, and your line was bodies that loved god. Which body did you treat with honor? Today, saints with a job description. Day nine hundred fifty-one.

Lost your keys? Some Catholics will tell you, half laughing and fully serious, to ask Saint Anthony. A small statue of Saint Joseph on a carpenter's workbench. A medal of Saint Christopher clipped to a car's sun visor. A doctor with a picture of Saint Luke in her locker. It can look like a phone directory of heaven: one saint per department. There's something truer underneath it, and today's word holds it.
screen: `ASK SAINT ANTHONY.` → `JOSEPH ON A WORKBENCH.` → `ONE SAINT PER DEPARTMENT?`

segments.voice: A patron saint is a saint Catholics ask to pray for a particular place, people, work or need. Countries have patrons, and cities, and parishes. So do jobs. Joseph, the carpenter, for workers. Luke, called a physician in a letter of Paul, for doctors. Cecilia, remembered for music, for musicians. Thomas More, the lawyer who refused to swear an oath against his conscience, for politicians. Sometimes a pope names a patron officially; sometimes the connection grew up among ordinary people over time. Underneath every patron is a simple idea from the letter of James. In the Douay-Rheims: "pray one for another, that you may be saved. For the continual prayer of a just man availeth much." Catholics believe the saints are alive with God, and so they can still do what friends do: pray for you. The Catechism says the saints don't stop interceding for us. A patron is not a replacement for God, and not a vending machine for favors. In Catholic teaching, asking a saint for help means asking that saint to pray with you, to God. Why a particular saint? Because they know the job. A saint who worked with wood knows splinters. A saint who was a doctor knows the night shift. Asking a patron is a little like asking a colleague who has done your work before, and done it with love, to put in a word. Not a department of heaven. A friend for the job.
screen: `A SAINT FOR A PLACE, A PEOPLE, A WORK.` · `JOSEPH, LUKE, CECILIA, THOMAS MORE.` · `PRAY ONE FOR ANOTHER.` · `A FRIEND WHO KNOWS THE JOB.` · then, large: `THE CONTINUAL PRAYER OF A JUST MAN AVAILETH MUCH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pick a patron for your work. Your work might be a job, or school, or raising children, or caring for someone, or looking for work. Settle into the sit and bring that work to mind: its hardest part, the hour of the day it weighs most. Later, look up a saint connected to it. For now, if you pray, you can ask any saint you already know to pray for you in that hard part. If you don't, simply hold your work in mind kindly, as something worth doing well. The bell holds the time.
Patron. A saint Catholics ask to pray for a particular place, people, work or need: a friend in heaven who knows the job.
Your line: a friend for the job. Today, ask someone who has done what you're doing for one piece of advice, and listen. Day nine hundred fifty-one.

952.title: The Litany of the Saints
952.hook: a long chant of names, sung at baptisms and ordinations: pray for us
952.howItsDone: The Litany of the Saints is sung at the Easter Vigil before baptisms and at ordinations while the candidates lie prostrate; a cantor sings each name and the congregation answers "pray for us".

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was patron, and your line was a friend for the job. Whose advice did you ask for? Today closes the week, with all those friends at once. Day nine hundred fifty-two.

A cathedral, full. At the front, a row of men in white lie face down on the stone floor, arms at their sides, not moving. They're about to be ordained priests. Above them, a cantor begins to sing names. Holy Mary. Saint Michael. Saint Peter, Saint Paul. And after each name the whole church sings back the same short answer. Name, answer. Name, answer. It goes on long enough that you stop counting and start listening. That chant is today's word.
screen: `MEN LYING FACE DOWN ON STONE.` → `A CANTOR SINGS NAMES.` → `THE CHURCH SINGS BACK.`

segments.voice: A litany is a prayer built from repetition: a leader calls out one line after another, and the people answer each time with the same response. The Litany of the Saints is the one the Church sings at some of its biggest moments. It's sung at the Easter Vigil before new Christians are baptized, and at ordinations while the candidates lie on the floor, as you just heard. It begins by asking the Lord for mercy. Then the names: Mary first, then angels, John the Baptist and Joseph, apostles, martyrs, bishops and teachers, monks and nuns, and at last all the holy men and women. After each name the answer is pray for us. It's an old request. Near the close of his first letter to the Thessalonians, Paul asks for it plainly, in the Douay-Rheims: "Brethren, pray for us." The litany turns that request toward the saints, in heaven. Parishes may add their own patrons, and the local saints of that place. Then the litany turns: it asks God directly to deliver his people, and to hear their prayer. Now look back at this week. You started with the saints of now: they're still here. Then the martyrology, a calendar with someone on every day. Canonization, tested then declared. Beatification, the long line. Relics, bodies that loved God. Patrons, friends for the job. The litany gathers all of it into one long breath. Every name was a life, tested and remembered, and a church full of people is asking each of them for one thing.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray five saints' names. Settle in. Pick five: Mary, perhaps, and four others you've met in this climb or love already. Say the first name slowly, in your head or out loud. If you pray, follow it with the litany's answer: pray for us. If you don't, follow it with one full breath. Then the next name, and the next. When you reach five, start again, slower. Let the rhythm carry you, name and answer, name and breath. The bell holds the time.
Litany. A prayer of many lines with one repeated answer; the Litany of the Saints calls the names of the saints and answers, pray for us.
Your line: pray for us. Today, if someone tells you they're struggling, ask them if there's one name, a person, they'd like you to remember for them. Day nine hundred fifty-two.
